title: MLB proposes compressing free agency window to 2-3 weeks; union calls it a 'player rights' elimination
dek: MLB has proposed shrinking the free agency signing window to just 2-3 weeks in December, with a freeze on all transactions until early February. The players' union says the plan, tied to a salary cap push, would strip player leverage and trigger lockout risk as the current CBA expires Dec. 1.
author: The GoCheckMySports Desk
key_fact: Free agency would open the Monday after the Winter Meetings in early December and close Dec. 21, with no signings or trades allowed until the first Monday in February.
bottom_line: The free agency window compression, paired with the salary cap push, marks MLB's most aggressive offseason restructuring bid. With Dec. 1 approaching and both sides entrenched, watch for either a counterproposal from the union or movement toward a lockout deadline.
body: MLB has proposed compressing the free agency signing window to 2-3 weeks in December, according to Yahoo Sports reporting on the league's latest CBA proposal. The window would open the Monday after the Winter Meetings in early December and close Dec. 21, with no free agency signings or trades permitted until the first Monday in February, per the reporting.

The proposal includes a "dead period" similar to the NFL's legal tampering window, during which players could negotiate with clubs but not sign, according to Yahoo Sports. Trades would be permitted before the first day of Winter Meetings during this period.

MLBPA interim executive director Bruce Meyer rejected the proposal as a violation of player rights. "Their latest proposals regarding free agency would eliminate player rights by establishing an artificial free agency window, subject to a salary cap, which would reduce player leverage and create a game of musical chairs pitting player vs. player," Meyer said in a statement reported by Yahoo Sports via The Athletic.

The compressed window is part of a broader CBA restructuring. MLB's May proposal featured a salary floor of $171.2 million and a cap of $245.3 million, per Yahoo Sports reporting. That cap proposal has been the central point of tension since negotiations began in April, according to the reporting. The current CBA expires Dec. 1.

Meyer added that the union has offered alternative changes to address roster churn and early free agent signing without a salary cap. "The suggestion that the only way to limit roster churn, or incentivize earlier free agent signing is with a salary cap is entirely unserious," he said, according to Yahoo Sports. "Players have proposed changes that would address these priorities, but the league is not interested in any changes that don't directly reduce the rights of all players and shift leverage to the owners."

Implementing the salary floor and cap would require dramatic payroll shifts across the league. The lowest-spending teams, like the Miami Marlins and Cleveland Guardians, would roughly double their payroll, while the highest-spending teams, including the Los Angeles Dodgers and New York Mets, would need to make significant cuts, according to Yahoo Sports reporting.

MLB has promoted the salary cap through a public campaign called "Level the Playing Field," which argues that narrowing the spending gap between teams would increase overall league competitiveness, per the reporting. The league has not released an official statement defending the free agency compression proposal beyond that campaign messaging.
